content:
jordan: Heads-up — I want to sync on the 'credit handoff' between admission and abuse. Found a few edge cases in the probe run where clients slid into probation but still consumed reservoir credits.
maya: Yeah saw that in the dashboard. Can you paste the trace id? :eyes:
jordan: trace=trace-9c2. Short summary: client A hit a short abuse spike, admission marked PROBATION but our token broker continued to hand out reserved burst credits for ~12s.
sam: Oh that sounds like a race between policy update and token reconciliation. Do we have order guarantees on the admission event -> token revoke path?
jordan: No strict order today. We send admission decision via control-plane pubsub, token-service listens and applies. But token-service also reconciles on interval and admits on local heuristics.
kelsey: I sketched two options in the RFC followup: 1) make admission authoritative (block until token-store ack) or 2) make admission a best-effort signal and tighten token TTLs. Tradeoffs: 1 adds latency to admission path; 2 increases false positives/evictions.
maya: For short probation windows (5-15s) blocking on ack seems reasonable. High-frequency decisions might be problematic for scale though.
tony: Another approach: incremental revoke: send a high-priority revoke marker that token-service processes immediately via a fastpath. If fastpath fails, fallback to reconcile.
jordan: fastpath sounds good. Implementation idea: admission publishes `revoke_v1` to kafka with partition key tenant_id and a small consumer group dedicated to revokes -> token-service consumes with priority HTTP push.
lucy: Quick note: we need to preserve telemetry so rollback is easy. Add `decision_id` and `issued_at` to the revoke event. Also include `grace_ms`.
sam: If we do fastpath, we should still accept eventual consistency — tokens may still land in-flight. So client-side should get `429` or `probation-warning` if their request hits admission while token persists.
kelsey: Agree. Also consider per-tenant borrow pools: if tenant has active borrow pool, revoke should target pool allocator to stop new borrows, then drain.
jordan: Implementation plan proposal: 1) add revoke_v1 event with metadata; 2) token-service implements priority consumer and stops new grants immediately; 3) add short-lived token-epoch header to active tokens so in-flight requests can be checked; 4) client path treats epoch mismatch as soft fail -> return 429 with retry-after.
maya: Can we avoid adding headers by checking token issue timestamp vs decision issued_at? That avoids protocol churn.
tony: That works for most cases but header approach helps in case token gets refreshed after decision due to clock skew. If we trust monotonic counters maybe ok.
lucy: I'll write a short test harness: simulate revoke + concurrent grants, measure window. Want to confirm worst-case leakage < 100ms.
infra-bot: deploy scheduled: canary token-service revokes v1 on staging at 2026-03-24T02:00Z
jordan: Thanks. Kelsey + Lucy can you pair on the fastpath consumer spec? I'll draft the follow-up RFC patch for admission blocking TTL options.
kelsey: Yep pairing now. Will push a design doc snippet and ping here. :thumbsup:
maya: we should add metrics: revoke-latency, grants-after-revoke, epoch-mismatch-count. Add alert if grants-after-revoke > 1/min.
sam: Also log correlated traces with `decision_id` so we can trace client->token flow.
jordan: Great. Closing loop: plan to land prototype on staging, run synthetic probe for 6h, then postmortem. Thanks all.
